nameStory: The "nosy" pill woodlouse gets its memorable name from a distinctive projection on its head that looks like a prominent nose! This little snout-like feature helps distinguish it from its more common cousin, the regular pill woodlouse. It's like nature gave this little armored creature a built-in identifying feature right on its face.
description: The nosy pill woodlouse is a small, gray-brown crustacean that looks like a tiny armadillo living under logs and rocks. Despite its name, it's not actually a bug at all, but rather a land-dwelling relative of shrimp and crabs! These oval-shaped creatures can roll into a perfect ball when threatened, and they're about the size of a large pea. Originally from Western Europe, they've made themselves quite at home in New England's gardens and forests.

idTips.label: Nose-like projection
idTips.description: Look for a small but noticeable bump or projection on the front of the head that resembles a tiny nose - this is the key feature that gives this species its name

idTips.label: Rolling ability
idTips.description: Can roll into a tight, smooth ball when disturbed - the ball feels firm and slightly cool to the touch, like a small marble

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Hard, segmented shell feels smooth and slightly waxy when gently touched, with visible plates that overlap like armor

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Usually gray to brownish-gray with sometimes a mottled appearance, occasionally with lighter edges on the body segments

idTips.label: Seven pairs of legs
idTips.description: When unrolled, you can count seven pairs of walking legs beneath the body - they move with a distinctive scuttling motion

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of antennae, with the longer pair being quite noticeable and active as they explore their surroundings

habitat: Look for nosy pill woodlice in moist, sheltered spots throughout New England's forests, gardens, and parks. They love hiding under rotting logs, leaf litter, mulch, and stones where the soil stays damp. You'll often find them in compost piles, under flower pots, or in the rich soil around foundation plantings where moisture collects.

seasonality.spring: Becomes active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots under deep leaf litter and logs. This is an excellent time to find them as they venture out to feed on decomposing plant material.
seasonality.summer: Most active during summer months, especially after rain when they come out to feed. Look for them in early morning or evening when moisture levels are higher.
seasonality.fall: Very active as they feed heavily on fallen leaves and prepare for winter. Often found in large numbers under fresh leaf litter and mulch piles.
seasonality.winter: Much less active, hiding deep in protected spots like under logs, in compost, or beneath thick leaf litter. Still findable on warmer winter days.

funFact: These little "pill bugs" actually breathe through gills, just like fish! They need to keep their gills moist to survive, which is why you'll always find them in damp places - they're basically land crabs that never fully left their aquatic roots behind.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the regular common pill woodlouse, but the nosy pill woodlouse has that distinctive nose-like bump on its head. Memory trick: "Nosy has a nose!" Also sometimes mistaken for sow bugs, but sow bugs cannot roll into a complete ball like pill woodlice can.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "pill bugs," "roly-polies," or "woodlice," these creatures aren't insects at all - they're actually crustaceans more closely related to lobsters than beetles! This explains why they need moist environments and have gills instead of the breathing holes that insects use.
compareHints: The nosy pill woodlouse is distinguished from its close relative, the common pill woodlouse, primarily by that prominent nose-like projection on its head. Both species can roll into balls and live in similar habitats, but the common pill woodlouse has a smooth, rounded head without the distinctive "nose." The nosy variety also tends to be slightly larger and may have more pronounced body segmentation.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Common Pill Woodlouse is distinguished from its relative the Nosy Pill Woodlouse by its more uniformly gray coloration and slightly larger size.
